4: Start with where the code sits.
The operator steps for retiring Group Policy are already written, in this workbook's own guidance.
This code serves two of them: importing every in-scope G P O into Group Policy analytics, and creating the policy library as code.
Two rules shape it, and both are this workbook's guidance.
One owning policy, and one owning tool, per setting, so the library holds only settings Intune owns.
And build unassigned: the code creates policies with no assignments, and assigning them is a later, reviewed step.
Its page on importing GPOs into Group Policy analytics says the tool is for Windows only, and imports G P O exports under four megabytes.
Its page on creating a settings catalog policy from imported GPOs calls the Migrate step best effort, and says it stops when two GPOs set one setting to different values.
And Learn's Microsoft Graph reference documents the migration reports and settings catalog policies in beta only.
5: Microsoft Learn's Intune migration guide points to Microsoft's Intune Graph samples, on GitHub, for exporting and importing policies, and says the scripts change your tenant and come as-is.
Their settings catalog folder has an import script.
The repository keeps a pinned copy, and a test harness runs it, unmodified, against a fake Graph.
The import creates the policy with one POST, unassigned.
But run it twice and it creates a second policy with the same name, because it never reads the tenant.
It sends to the worldwide Graph host whatever cloud you signed in to, and Learn's page on Microsoft Graph national cloud deployments gives each cloud its own host.
It uses whatever session you opened, whatever its scopes.
It silently strips service-set properties, so the body sent isn't the file reviewed.
And it records nothing beyond the screen.
The example adds a sync that reads the tenant first, a host per cloud, a read-only scope for the dry run, refusals instead of silent edits, and a sync record.
6: The read side has two parts.
The validation kit's check reads the migration reports, and fails on any G P O targeted in Active Directory whose readiness isn't complete, and on any in-scope G P O that was never imported.
It works per G P O, and doesn't read the settings.
The move plan works per setting.
It reads each report's setting mappings, which Learn's Graph beta reference documents, and gives every row a disposition.
The dispositions are the kit's design.
A candidate is supported and has an Intune setting definition, and a person decides whether it moves.
A conflict is two GPOs setting one definition to different values: Learn's page on creating a settings catalog policy from imported GPOs says Migrate stops on that case.
The decision record picks the value.
AppLocker and firewall settings go to Endpoint security, as that page says.
And, in this workbook's guidance, the plan decides nothing: Group Policy analytics finds the landing zone, never whether a setting is still needed.
7: Each settings catalog policy is a jay-son file.
The policy part is the body Graph receives, exactly as reviewed, in the shape Microsoft Learn's Graph beta reference documents for creating a configuration policy.
The rest is the record: who approves a change, which tool owns the settings, which GPOs they came from, and the I D of each setting's decision record.
The linter applies ten rules, and they're the kit's design.
GPC oh two: the config owner must be Intune, because a setting another tool owns stays with that tool.
GPC oh six: one setting definition in one policy, because two policies on one setting is a conflict.
GPC oh nine: every setting has a decision record.
And GPC oh eight, with the move plan: a setting that isn't a candidate is shown, with its decision.
GPC ten warns on a value that looks like a secret: Learn's page on device profiles says anyone who can read device configuration can read such values.
8: The sync is the kit's design.
It reads the tenant's settings catalog policies, through the list call Learn's Graph beta reference documents, normalizes both sides, and gives each library policy one action.
Create: it isn't in the tenant.
No change: the same settings, description, platform, technology and scope tags.
Drift: it differs, and the row names each setting that changed.
Duplicate: two tenant policies have the library's name.
Without the apply option, the sync is a dry run: it signs in with read only, and sends only GET.
With apply, it signs in with read-write, POSTs each create, reads it back and compares again.
And it writes nothing at all if the lint has a finding, or any policy is drift or duplicate.
It never sends PATCH or DELETE, although Learn documents both.
A policy that differs from Git is a decision for a person, and, in this workbook's guidance, a change becomes a new version under a new name.
